newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Belgian PM set to present 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Belgian PM set to present 1997 budget.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene was set on Tuesday to present his 1997 budget to parliament and set out Belgium's case for membership of a European single currency.
"The prime minister will present a budget which will allow us to enter monetary union," Budget Minister Herman Van Rompuy told VTM television.

In his budget speech, starting at 1300 GMT, Dehaene was expected to announce the 1997 budget would cut the public deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, from a 3.0 percent target in 1996.
Most of the measures in the 80 billion franc ($2.55 billion) austerity package leaked out before last weekend, and the Belgian press has been fiercely critical.

"This long list of tiny measures here and there will not really hurt anyone...The government's action seems to be motivated by the desire not to upset anyone, rather than working for a better society," said the Catholic daily La Libre Belgique.
The budget package contains 30 billion francs of increases in indirect taxes, mainly on petrol, alcohol and cigarettes.
Spending cuts worth 50 billion francs will claw away at the pension, unemployment, child and health benefits of Belgium's generous social security system.

But besides the gradual increase of women's retirement age to 65 from 60 over a 13-year period, most other measures are so technical that specialists have had trouble explaining them. They largely consist of blocking future rises in benefits rather than scaling back existing ones.
"The Maastricht project has been reached, but with a disputable budget...the promise of a fundamental reform of the social security has not been kept," said financial daily L'Echo.
The Maastricht Treaty sets the economic targets that EU countries must meet to join economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
Social Affairs Minister Magda De Galan defended the budget, telling VTM: "It is an equitable budget which contains the germs of a long-term cleanup of state finances."

Dehaene is also expected to announce a number of "one-shot" measures worth an additional 20 billion francs. They could include central bank gains on a renewal of 100-franc bank notes and a plan to privatise a further 25 percent of bank ASLK-CGER.
Dehaene is seen likely to also use the budget speech to announce that central bank reserves will be used to buy back debt.
While Belgium scores well on the Maastricht Treaty criteria for inflation, currency stability, interest rates and deficit, the country's huge 9.828 trillion franc debt remains a problem.

Central bank governor Alfons Verplaetse said earlier this month that 236 billion francs worth of capital gains on gold sales and other asset sales in recent years could be used to repay about 300 billion francs worth of foreign currency debt.
A reserves-for-debt swap could reduce Belgium's debt to GDP ratio, which without any action is forecast to be 131.8 percent of 1996 GDP, the highest in the EU.
Budget Minister Van Rompuy said Dehaene would also make a statement about political murder and paedophile scandals which have rocked the country recently.
As soon as his budget is out of the way, Dehaene faces the daunting task of reforming the police and judiciary. Both have been hit by reports of blunders and infighting over the two scandals.
"Belgium is in the middle of a confidence crisis. The government must try to restore faith in our institutions," said L'Echo. ($1=31.36 Belgian Franc)
